title: The Son
focus: the pain of a father's love

teacherSummary.text: Siddhartha's spoiled son, raised in wealth, despises the ferry life and his father's gentleness. Vasudeva advises letting the boy return to the world, but Siddhartha cannot let go. The son finally runs away, stealing the ferry money. Siddhartha follows to the city and stops at Kamala's old garden, realizing he must not pursue him. Vasudeva brings him home.

items.prompt: Synthesis: trace how love and attachment develops from Sansara to The Son. Use one quotation from each.

questions.expected: Vasudeva's question implies that no one can be spared their own path; Siddhartha made his own mistakes and learned from them, so protecting his son would take away the only way to learn. Expected link: love and attachment, and the novel's claim about teaching versus experience.

questions.q: How does this line connect to love and attachment?
questions.expected: A father's love becomes his "final wound." (Vasudeva's question: each must find his own way.)

segments.script: Annotate the chapter for characterization, irony (three marks with a margin note each), then write one claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph: what does this chapter suggest about the pain of a father's love? Then start your writing prompt at your assigned level (HS Sophomore: Analyze how The Son develops the idea of the pain of a father's love. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of characterization and irony shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim. (You are reading the English translation by Gunther Olesch, Anke Dreher, Amy Coulter, Stefan Langer and Semyon Chaichenets, so word-choice evidence is the translators' English.)) Exemplar: Siddhartha's love for his son repeats his father's love for him, showing the cycle of attachment. When the text says “Would you actually believe that you had committed your foolish acts in order to spare your son from committing them too” (The Son, paragraph 14), it shows this directly. Vasudeva asks whether he committed "foolish acts in order to spare your son from committing them too," reminding him that he, too, left his father.

objective: Students will analyze how characterization develops in “The Son” by writing a claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph that cites at least 2 quotations from the section, and will score at least 80% on the section quiz.

routine: Bell-ringer: post one literal and one evaluative question; students jot before talking (wait time).
Discussion (10 min): run the focus questions for the class level in order, literal to evaluative; think-pair-share every DOK 3/4 item.

items.text: Which line of Kamala’s does Siddhartha remember when the boy’s face reminds him of her?
items.lookFor: “You cannot love”
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?
items.answerGuidance: “‘You cannot love,’ she had said to him, and he had agreed with her” (The Son, paragraph 17).

items.text: What image does Vasudeva use for the boy’s old life?
items.lookFor: A young bird used to a different nest
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?
items.answerGuidance: A bird from another nest: “That young bird is accustomed to a different life, to a different nest.” (The Son, paragraph 5)

items.text: What does the boy do after his outburst of rage?
items.lookFor: He runs away and returns late at night
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?
items.answerGuidance: He leaves and comes back only at night: “Then the boy ran away and only returned late at night.” (The Son, paragraph 22)

items.text: What does Siddhartha ask Vasudeva when they set out with the raft?
items.lookFor: Why he brought the axe
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?
items.answerGuidance: About the axe: “Why did you take the axe along?” asked Siddhartha. (The Son, paragraph 27)

items.text: What does Siddhartha feel at the garden gate instead of the goal he hoped for?
items.lookFor: Emptiness
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?
items.answerGuidance: Emptiness and sadness: “Instead of the desired goal, which had drawn him here following the runaway son, there was now emptiness.” (The Son, paragraph 34)

items.text: Retell the three most important events of “The Son” in order, in one sentence each.
items.lookFor: Siddhartha's spoiled son, raised in wealth, despises the ferry life and his father's gentleness. Vasudeva advises letting the boy return to the world, but Siddhartha cannot let go. The son finally runs away, stealing the ferry money. Siddhartha follows to the city and stops at Kamala's old garden, realizing he must not pursue him. Vasudeva brings him home.
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?
items.answerGuidance: The grieving boy refuses his father’s patient love (The Son, paragraphs 1–4); Siddhartha rejects Vasudeva’s advice to let him go (paragraphs 12–16); the boy rages, steals the fare money and runs away, and Siddhartha follows him to Kamala’s garden and stops (paragraphs 20–33).

items.text: Which characters appear or are mentioned in “The Son”? Name two and one thing each says or does.
items.lookFor: Names and actions taken from the chapter; check against the teacher summary.
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?
items.answerGuidance: Two of: the son, who shouts “I’m not your servant” (paragraph 21); Vasudeva, who advises letting him go and goes with Siddhartha to the city (paragraphs 12, 35); Kamala, remembered at her garden gate (paragraph 31).

items.text: Where and when does “The Son” take place? Point to the line that tells you.
items.lookFor: A place/time detail quoted from the chapter.
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?
items.answerGuidance: At the ferry over months, then the city road and Kamala’s old garden: “For a long time, for long months, Siddhartha waited for his son to understand him” (The Son, paragraph 4)… and paragraph 31 for the garden.

items.text: Reread: “For a long time, for long months, Siddhartha waited for his son to understand him, to accept his love, to perhaps reciprocate it.” What does “reciprocate” mean here, and what is literally happening in this line?
items.lookFor: reciprocate: to return (a feeling).
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?
items.answerGuidance: “Reciprocate” here means: to return (a feeling). In The Son, paragraph 4, the word names his long waiting; literally, Siddhartha waits month after month for the boy to accept his love and return it, and it does not happen.

items.text: Reread: “‘I must follow him,’ said Siddhartha, who had been shivering with grief since those ranting speeches the boy had made yesterday.” What does “ranting” mean here, and what is literally happening in this line?
items.lookFor: ranting: loud and angry.
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?
items.answerGuidance: “Ranting” here means: loud and angry. In The Son, paragraph 24, Siddhartha has been “shivering with grief” since his son’s raging speech; literally, he insists on following the boy who has run away with the boat.

items.text: What does “The Son” suggest about the pain of a father's love? State the inference and the line that supports it.
items.lookFor: A stated inference (for example, that a father’s love is both foolish and necessary) backed by one located line, such as the one in The Son, paragraph 18.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: The chapter suggests a father’s love is both foolish and necessary. Support: “Nevertheless, he felt at the same time, it was not worthless, it was necessary, came from the essence of his own being.” (The Son, paragraph 18)

items.text: Find one example of characterization in this chapter. What does it reveal that a plain statement would not?
items.lookFor: Look for what characters say, do and think, and how others react to them.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: The boy is characterized at the funeral and after (“Pale, he sat for many days by the hill of the dead, did not want to eat” (The Son, paragraph 1)): grief and pride, shown in actions, explain his later rage better than a label would.

items.text: How does the irony in this chapter shape what we understand about the pain of a father's love?
items.lookFor: Look for gaps between what characters expect or say and what is true.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: The irony is that Siddhartha now lives what he left: like his own father, he cannot hold a son who wants to go, and like the childlike people, he is ruled by passion (The Son, paragraph 18).

items.text: In the passage that begins “For a long time, for long months, Siddhartha waited for his son to understand him, to accept his love, to perhaps reciprocate it.”, why might Hesse have chosen these particular words? Pick two and explain their connotations.
items.lookFor: Diction analysis of two words in the anchor passage.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: In The Son, paragraph 4, “for a long time, for long months” stretches the wait by repetition; “waited” makes his love passive and patient, which the boy reads as weakness.

items.text: What causes the main turn in “The Son”, and what effect is it likely to have on what follows?
items.lookFor: Siddhartha's spoiled son, raised in wealth, despises the ferry life and his father's gentleness. Vasudeva advises letting the boy return to the world, but Siddhartha cannot let go. The son finally runs away, stealing the ferry money. Siddhartha follows to the city and stops at Kamala's old garden,…
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: The cause is the boy’s outburst and flight (The Son, paragraphs 20–23). Effect: Siddhartha learns he cannot keep him (paragraph 33) and carries the wound into the next chapter.

items.text: How does “The Son” build on “The Ferryman”? Name one link of cause and effect.
items.lookFor: A causal or structural link between this and the previous chapter.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Cause and effect: at the end of “The Ferryman” Kamala died and left the boy; here that gift becomes his deepest pain, “Rich and happy, he had called himself, when the boy had come to him.” (The Son, paragraph 3)

items.text: What can we infer about a character's motives from what they say and do here, as opposed to what they claim?
items.lookFor: An inference about motive supported by a quoted line.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Siddhartha claims patience, but his clinging shows need (“Siddhartha could not heed his friend’s advice, he could not give up the boy.” (The Son, paragraph 16)); the boy claims hatred, but grief for his mother drives it (paragraph 1).

items.text: The bell-ringer asked: “How does Siddhartha's situation mirror his own father's?” Now that we have read closely, how would you revise your first answer, and which line changed your mind?
items.lookFor: A revised answer anchored in the text.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: A revised answer should line up the two departures: Siddhartha left his father at night in “The Son of the Brahmin”; now his son leaves him the same way (The Son, paragraph 23), and he must accept it (paragraph 33).

items.text: Where does the theme of love and attachment appear most clearly in this chapter, and how does it connect to the rest of the book?
items.lookFor: A located moment where Siddhartha’s love for his son turns into clinging, linked to one earlier chapter.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: The theme of love and attachment appears where he sees he cannot live for another: “he could not help his son, that he was not allowed to cling him” (The Son, paragraph 33).

items.text: Background: This chapter reverses Chapter One: now Siddhartha is the father whose son leaves. How does knowing this change the way you read one moment in the chapter?
items.lookFor: A specific moment reread in light of the context.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Knowing the chapter reverses Chapter One lets students read the father’s side: Siddhartha now feels what his father felt the night he stood in the chamber (compare paragraph 33 with “The Son of the Brahmin,” paragraph 47).

items.text: A critic might argue: “Siddhartha experiences foolish, painful love—the very attachment he once found childlike.” How far do you agree? Take a stand and defend it with two lines from the chapter.
items.lookFor: A defended position with evidence and one counterpoint.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: Agree: he experiences the passion he despised (The Son, paragraph 18). A text counterpoint: he judges it “not worthless” and “necessary” in the same paragraph, so the chapter does not simply call it a fall.

items.text: Which character in this chapter acts most wisely, and which least? Judge them by a standard you name.
items.lookFor: An evaluation using an explicit criterion and evidence.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: With wisdom as letting go, Vasudeva is wisest (paragraph 12); Siddhartha least when he refuses that advice (paragraph 16), though the boy’s theft (paragraph 23) is the least wise act.

items.text: Rewrite one moment of “The Son” from the point of view of a different character. What does the new angle reveal or hide about the pain of a father's love?
items.lookFor: A rewrite that keeps the chapter’s events accurate, speaks in the chosen character’s voice, and ends with a sentence on what the new angle shows or hides.
followUps: Which line from the chapter does your piece depend on? Read it to us.
What did you keep from the original, and what did you change on purpose?
items.answerGuidance: The son’s view of his outburst (The Son, paragraphs 20–22) works well: it shows how suffocating patience can feel and hides how much his father loves him.

items.text: Write three questions of your own about “The Son”: one recall, one “why/how”, and one “should/what if”. Trade with a partner and answer theirs.
items.lookFor: Three questions at three levels, each answerable from the chapter, traded and answered with a line.
followUps: Which of your three questions was hardest to answer from the text, and why?
Which line did your partner use, and does it really answer your why/how question?
items.answerGuidance: Example set: recall, ‘What does the boy take?’ (the fare basket and boat, paragraph 23); why/how, ‘Why won’t Siddhartha let him go?’ (paragraph 18); what if, ‘Should Siddhartha have taken him to the city?’

items.text: Connect this chapter to the search for self-knowledge: is the link strong or weak so far? What would Hesse need to show next to strengthen it?
items.lookFor: A judgment of thematic development across the work.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: Strong: he learns about himself through love, not teaching (paragraph 18). Hesse needs to show the wound healing into insight, which “Om” does.

items.text: Is the characterization in this chapter effective, or does it feel heavy-handed? Evaluate it as a reader would in a review.
items.lookFor: An evaluative judgment with criteria and evidence.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: Effective: the boy is drawn through actions and his outburst (paragraphs 1, 21). Some readers find the outburst exaggerated.

items.text: Compare how “The Son” treats the pain of a father's love with how another text, film or event you know treats a similar idea. What does Siddhartha see that the other misses?
items.lookFor: A cross-text synthesis.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: A comparison should name a story of a parent and a rebellious child and quote “he could not help his son, that he was not allowed to cling him” (The Son, paragraph 33); Siddhartha’s case adds that he once did the same to his father.

items.text: Predict what “Om” will bring, using two clues from this chapter. After reading, evaluate your prediction.
items.lookFor: A prediction or judgment justified with textual clues.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: Clues: the wound has “not been given to him in order to turn the knife in it” (The Son, paragraph 33), and Vasudeva brings him home (paragraph 35). Prediction: he will turn his grief into understanding with the river’s help.

items.text: Design a one-paragraph modern adaptation of this chapter (setting, characters, conflict). What must stay the same for it to still be about the pain of a father's love?
items.lookFor: A modern setting, characters and conflict that keep the chapter’s core idea, with the one element that must not change named.
followUps: Which line from the chapter does your piece depend on? Read it to us.
What did you keep from the original, and what did you change on purpose?
items.answerGuidance: A modern version keeps a wise, patient parent and a grieving, angry teenager who runs off. What must stay is the parent’s realization that he cannot hold the child (paragraph 33).

items.text: What question would you most like to ask Hermann Hesse about this chapter, and what answer do you think the text itself gives?
items.lookFor: A student-generated question answered from evidence.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: Example: ‘Did Siddhartha fail as a father?’ The text says his love was blind but necessary (The Son, paragraph 18).

Explain a father’s love for a son he cannot protect from his own path, using “But even if you would die ten times for him, you would not be able to take the slightest part of his destiny upon yourself.” (Hesse, 1922/2015, The Son, para. 14), and compare one critical voice from this unit.

Apply a formal reading to a father’s love for a son he cannot protect from his own path: show how imagery and repetition in “But even if you would die ten times for him, you would not be able to take the slightest part of his destiny upon yourself.” (Hesse, 1922/2015, The Son, para. 14) build its meaning.

Argue how a father’s love for a son he cannot protect from his own path advances the novel’s claim about teaching versus experience, testing “But even if you would die ten times for him, you would not be able to take the slightest part of his destiny upon yourself.” (Hesse, 1922/2015, The Son, para. 14) against one later chapter.

Situate a father’s love for a son he cannot protect from his own path within scholarship on Hesse and European representations of Indian thought, stating method and contribution, with “But even if you would die ten times for him, you would not be able to take the slightest part of his destiny upon yourself.” (Hesse, 1922/2015, The Son, para. 14) as anchor.
